title: Given a Scenario, Install and Configure Motherboards, CPUs, and Add-On Cards

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Installing a motherboard or CPU requires more than finding a part that appears to fit. You must select compatible hardware, connect it correctly, configure firmware and security settings, install the required expansion capability, and provide effective cooling.
bullets: Motherboard form factor and connector types
sections.callout: FIT → CONNECT → COMPATIBILITY → CONFIGURE → EXPAND → COOL

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: When a scenario describes a motherboard, CPU, firmware setting, expansion requirement, or cooling problem, identify which layer must be installed or configured before choosing a solution.
bullets: CPU heat transfer → heat sink plus thermal interface material

sections.title: Motherboard Form Factors
paragraphs: A motherboard form factor defines physical dimensions, mounting layout, general expansion capacity, and case compatibility. Objective 3.5 requires Advanced Technology Extended (ATX), microATX, and Information Technology eXtended (ITX).
sections.callout: Form factor answers: how large is the board, and what case supports it?

sections.title: Advanced Technology Extended (ATX)
paragraphs: ATX is a common full-size desktop motherboard form factor. Its larger area generally allows more expansion slots, connectors, and components.
sections.callout: Desktop build needing substantial expansion capability → ATX.

sections.title: microATX
paragraphs: microATX is smaller than standard ATX and is used when a system needs a compact desktop design while retaining common desktop components. It generally offers fewer expansion slots than ATX.
sections.callout: Smaller desktop build with moderate expansion needs → microATX.

sections.title: Information Technology eXtended (ITX)
paragraphs: ITX identifies a family of compact motherboard designs. In typical PC-building scenarios, Mini-ITX is the commonly encountered implementation and prioritizes a small system footprint over physical expansion capacity.
sections.callout: Very compact desktop system → ITX.

sections.title: ATX vs. microATX vs. ITX
sections.callout: Always verify that the case supports the motherboard form factor.

sections.title: Motherboard Connector Types
paragraphs: Motherboards provide connectors for expansion cards, storage, power, internal devices, case controls, and compact modules.

sections.title: Peripheral Component Interconnect (PCI)
paragraphs: PCI is an older expansion bus historically used for sound cards, network cards, and other add-on hardware.
sections.callout: Legacy motherboard expansion slot → PCI.

sections.title: PCIe Expansion
paragraphs: Peripheral Component Interconnect Express (PCIe) is the modern high-speed serial expansion interface for video cards, network cards, sound cards, capture cards, and some storage devices. Slots can use lane configurations such as x1, x4, x8, and x16.
sections.callout: Modern graphics or expansion card → PCIe.

sections.title: PCI vs. PCIe
sections.callout: PCI = legacy. PCIe = modern.

sections.title: Power Connectors
paragraphs: The motherboard requires power from the power supply through the main motherboard connector and commonly a separate CPU power connector near the processor socket. Both connections must be seated correctly.
sections.callout: Newly assembled system is completely dead → verify motherboard and CPU power connections.

sections.title: SATA Motherboard Connector
paragraphs: Serial Advanced Technology Attachment (SATA) motherboard ports connect internal hard drives, SATA SSDs, and optical drives.
sections.callout: Internal SATA storage connection → SATA port.

sections.title: eSATA Motherboard Connector
paragraphs: External SATA (eSATA) provides SATA-based connectivity for external storage.
sections.callout: SATA = internal. eSATA = external.

sections.title: Headers
paragraphs: A header is a group of motherboard pins used to connect internal components or case features. Common examples include front-panel buttons, status LEDs, USB ports, audio, and fans.
sections.callout: Case power button or LED connection → front-panel header.

sections.title: M.2 Motherboard Connector
paragraphs: M.2 is a compact motherboard connector and module form factor used for SSDs, wireless cards, and other compact devices. An M.2 storage device may use SATA or PCIe/NVMe depending on the module and slot.
sections.callout: M.2 identifies the compact physical connection; it does not automatically mean NVMe.

sections.title: Motherboard Compatibility
paragraphs: Before installing a CPU, verify the manufacturer platform, physical socket, supported processor generation, chipset, and BIOS/UEFI support. Physical fit by itself does not guarantee electrical or firmware compatibility.
sections.callout: CPU → SOCKET → CHIPSET → FIRMWARE SUPPORT

sections.title: CPU Socket Types
paragraphs: The CPU socket provides the physical and electrical connection between processor and motherboard. AMD and Intel each use multiple socket designs across product generations.
sections.callout: Buying a replacement CPU → verify the exact socket first.

sections.title: AMD and Intel Socket Compatibility

entries.title: AMD Socket Compatibility
paragraphs: An AMD motherboard does not support every AMD processor. Confirm the socket, chipset, processor generation, and BIOS/UEFI support.

entries.title: Intel Socket Compatibility
paragraphs: An Intel motherboard does not support every Intel processor. Confirm the socket, chipset, processor generation, and BIOS/UEFI support.

sections.callout: CPU brand alone does not prove compatibility.

sections.title: Multisocket Motherboards
paragraphs: A multisocket motherboard supports more than one physical CPU. These boards are most common in servers, high-end workstations, and specialized systems.
sections.callout: Multiple physical processors → multisocket motherboard.

sections.title: Multisocket vs. Multicore

table.caption: Physical processors and internal processing units
rows: More than one physical CPU socket
Multiple processing cores inside one CPU package

sections.callout: SOCKET = physical CPU. CORE = processing unit inside the CPU.

sections.title: BIOS/UEFI Settings
paragraphs: BIOS or Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) initializes hardware and provides low-level configuration before the operating system loads. Modern systems generally use UEFI, while older systems commonly used legacy BIOS.
sections.callout: BIOS/UEFI = hardware configuration before the OS.

sections.title: Boot Options
paragraphs: Boot options control where and how the computer tries to load an operating system. The boot order can prioritize an internal drive, USB device, optical media, or the network.
sections.callout: Install an OS from USB → configure the firmware boot order.

sections.title: USB Permissions
paragraphs: Firmware settings may enable, disable, or restrict USB functionality for security and device control before the operating system loads.
sections.callout: Restrict USB at the firmware level → BIOS/UEFI USB permissions.

sections.title: TPM Security Features
paragraphs: A Trusted Platform Module (TPM) provides hardware-backed security functions. It can protect cryptographic keys and support device security, encryption, platform integrity, and secure authentication.
sections.callout: Hardware-backed key protection tied to the computer → TPM.

sections.title: Fan Considerations
paragraphs: BIOS/UEFI can configure or monitor fan speeds, fan profiles, and temperature-based behavior. Correct fan connections and firmware controls help maintain safe operating temperatures.
sections.callout: Adjust CPU fan behavior based on temperature → firmware fan settings.

sections.title: Secure Boot
paragraphs: Secure Boot is a UEFI security feature that helps prevent unauthorized or untrusted software from loading during startup.
sections.callout: Prevent an untrusted bootloader from starting → Secure Boot.

sections.title: TPM vs. Secure Boot
sections.callout: TPM protects security material; Secure Boot validates startup software.

sections.title: Boot Password and BIOS Password

entries.title: Boot Password
paragraphs: A boot password requires authentication before the system proceeds through startup.
entries.recognitionCue: Password required to start or use the machine → boot password.

entries.title: BIOS Password
paragraphs: A BIOS/UEFI password protects access to firmware configuration and prevents unauthorized settings changes.
entries.recognitionCue: Protect the firmware setup screen → BIOS password.

sections.callout: BOOT = start the computer. BIOS = change firmware settings.

sections.title: Temperature Monitoring
paragraphs: BIOS/UEFI can report CPU and system temperatures. Temperature data helps identify failed fans, poor airflow, incorrect cooler installation, and other thermal problems.
sections.callout: CPU shuts down under load → inspect temperature monitoring and cooling.

sections.title: Virtualization Support
paragraphs: Modern CPUs can provide hardware-assisted virtualization so one physical computer can run multiple virtual machines efficiently. The processor must support the feature, and the BIOS/UEFI setting may need to be enabled.
bullets: Intel VT-x and AMD-V are vendor examples.
The exam concept is CPU virtualization support plus firmware enablement.
sections.callout: Hypervisor says hardware virtualization is unavailable → verify CPU support and the firmware setting.

sections.title: Hardware Encryption
paragraphs: Objective 3.5 includes TPM and Hardware Security Module (HSM) as hardware that protects cryptographic keys and operations. Their intended scale and placement differ.
sections.callout: Identify whether the scenario needs endpoint platform security or dedicated cryptographic hardware.

sections.title: Trusted Platform Module (TPM)
paragraphs: A TPM is integrated into or closely associated with an individual computing platform. It can securely store or protect cryptographic information used by that endpoint.
sections.callout: Local platform encryption and key protection → TPM.

sections.title: Hardware Security Module (HSM)
paragraphs: A Hardware Security Module (HSM) is dedicated hardware designed to perform cryptographic operations and protect high-value keys. HSMs are associated with centralized or specialized security environments.
sections.callout: Dedicated hardware for high-value cryptographic keys → HSM.

sections.title: TPM vs. HSM

table.caption: Hardware-backed cryptographic security
rows: Device security and local key protection

sections.callout: TPM = device security. HSM = dedicated key security.

sections.title: CPU Architecture
paragraphs: CPU architecture defines the processor's instruction-set architecture and affects operating-system and software compatibility. Objective 3.5 requires x86/x64, ARM, and core configurations.
sections.callout: Architecture affects which software can execute on the processor.

sections.title: x86/x64
paragraphs: x86 commonly refers to the traditional 32-bit PC architecture. x64 is the 64-bit extension of the x86 family and supports a much larger address space. Modern desktops and laptops commonly use x64.
sections.callout: x86 = 32-bit clue. x64 = 64-bit x86-family clue.

sections.title: Advanced RISC Machine (ARM)
paragraphs: ARM is a Reduced Instruction Set Computer architecture widely used in mobile devices, tablets, embedded systems, and increasing numbers of computers and servers. ARM designs are strongly associated with power efficiency.
sections.callout: Power-efficient architecture common in mobile and embedded systems → ARM.

sections.title: x86/x64 vs. ARM

table.caption: Processor-architecture recognition
rows: Software must support x86 or x64 as appropriate

sections.callout: Choose by architecture requirement, not simply by how new the device is.

sections.title: Core Configurations
paragraphs: A CPU core is an individual processing unit inside a physical processor. A processor can have one or many cores, such as dual-core, quad-core, six-core, eight-core, or higher.
sections.callout: Multiple cores = multiple processing units inside one CPU package.

sections.title: Core Count vs. Clock Speed
paragraphs: Core count is the number of processing cores; clock speed is the rate at which processor cycles occur. More cores do not guarantee that every workload completes faster because software must be able to use them.
sections.callout: Cores = workers. Clock speed = pace.

sections.title: Expansion Cards
paragraphs: Expansion cards add capabilities to a computer. Modern sound, video, capture, and network interface cards commonly use PCIe.
sections.callout: Identify the capability the system needs to add.

sections.title: Sound Card
paragraphs: A sound card provides audio processing and audio input/output connections for speakers, headphones, microphones, and other audio equipment.
sections.callout: Additional audio capability → sound card.

sections.title: Video Card
paragraphs: A video card, or graphics card, contains a graphics processing unit (GPU) that renders graphics and produces display output.
sections.callout: Stronger 3D graphics or display output → video card.

sections.title: Capture Card
paragraphs: A capture card receives incoming audio/video signals so a computer can record, process, or stream them. Common uses include gameplay capture, camera input, streaming, and video production.
sections.callout: Record HDMI output from another device → capture card.

sections.title: Video Card vs. Capture Card

table.caption: Graphics output and external video input

sections.callout: VIDEO = OUT. CAPTURE = IN.

sections.title: Network Interface Card
paragraphs: A Network Interface Card (NIC) adds network connectivity, such as an additional Ethernet interface.
sections.callout: Additional network connection → NIC.

sections.title: Cooling
paragraphs: Computer components generate heat, and the CPU requires effective cooling to prevent thermal throttling, instability, shutdown, and hardware damage.

sections.title: Fans
paragraphs: A fan moves air through or around the computer to carry heat away. Fans support CPU cooling, case airflow, GPU cooling, and power-supply cooling.
sections.callout: Temperature rises because air is not moving → inspect fans and airflow.

sections.title: Heat Sink
paragraphs: A heat sink is a thermally conductive component that draws heat from a processor or chip and spreads it across a larger surface area for dissipation. A fan often moves air across its fins.
sections.callout: Heat sink = conduct and spread heat.

sections.title: Thermal Paste/Pads
paragraphs: Thermal paste fills microscopic imperfections between a CPU and heat sink to improve heat transfer. Thermal pads serve a similar thermal-interface role where a preformed material is appropriate.
bullets: Use the material specified for the hardware design.
Too little, too much, or incorrect installation can reduce cooling effectiveness.
Thermal interface material is not ordinary adhesive.
sections.callout: Thermal paste or pad helps heat move from component to cooler.

sections.title: Heat Sink vs. Thermal Interface Material
sections.callout: Thermal material transfers; the heat sink dissipates.

sections.title: Liquid Cooling
paragraphs: Liquid cooling uses coolant to carry heat from a cold plate or water block to a radiator, where fans release that heat into the air. A typical loop includes a cold plate, pump, tubing, radiator, fans, and coolant.
sections.callout: CPU → cold plate → coolant → radiator → air.

sections.title: Air Cooling vs. Liquid Cooling

table.caption: Common CPU cooling designs
rows: Pump failure can cause rapid temperature rise

sections.callout: Air = heat sink. Liquid = radiator loop.

sections.title: CPU Cooling Installation
bullets: Verify CPU, socket, and cooler compatibility.
Install the CPU in the correct orientation.
Apply or verify the appropriate thermal interface material.
Seat and secure the heat sink or cooling block evenly.
Connect required fan and pump power.
sections.callout: CONTACT → SECURE → POWER → VERIFY

sections.title: Objective 3.5 Exam Trap
paragraphs: Objective 3.5 mixes physical installation, firmware configuration, CPU architecture, security, expansion hardware, and cooling. Identify the layer the scenario tests before comparing answers.

entries.title: ATX vs. microATX vs. ITX
paragraphs: ATX generally offers the most physical expansion, microATX balances size and expansion, and ITX prioritizes compact size.

entries.title: PCI vs. PCIe
paragraphs: PCI is legacy; PCIe is the modern expansion interface.
entries.memoryHook: A modern GPU points to PCIe

entries.title: SATA vs. M.2
paragraphs: SATA identifies a storage interface; M.2 identifies a compact connector/form factor. An M.2 drive may use SATA or PCIe/NVMe.

entries.title: Manufacturer vs. Socket
paragraphs: AMD or Intel branding is not enough. Socket, chipset/platform, processor generation, and firmware support must match.

entries.title: Multisocket vs. Multicore
paragraphs: Multisocket means multiple physical CPUs; multicore means multiple processing units inside one CPU.
entries.memoryHook: Sockets = chips; cores = workers inside a chip

entries.title: TPM vs. Secure Boot
paragraphs: TPM provides hardware-backed cryptographic security; Secure Boot verifies trusted startup software.

entries.title: TPM vs. HSM
paragraphs: TPM is tied to an individual platform; HSM is dedicated cryptographic hardware.

entries.title: Boot Password vs. BIOS Password
paragraphs: A boot password controls system startup; a BIOS password controls access to firmware configuration.

entries.title: x86 vs. x64
paragraphs: x86 is the common 32-bit clue; x64 identifies the 64-bit x86-family architecture.

entries.title: x64 vs. ARM
paragraphs: x64 belongs to the traditional x86-family PC/server ecosystem; ARM is strongly associated with RISC-based power-efficient designs.

entries.title: Video Card vs. Capture Card
paragraphs: A video card renders output; a capture card receives external video.

entries.title: Fan vs. Heat Sink
paragraphs: A fan moves air; a heat sink conducts and spreads heat. They commonly work together.

entries.title: Heat Sink vs. Thermal Paste
paragraphs: The heat sink dissipates heat; thermal paste improves contact between the CPU and cooler.

entries.title: Air vs. Liquid Cooling
paragraphs: Air cooling uses a heat sink and fan; liquid cooling uses a pump, coolant, radiator, and fans.

sections.title: Installation and Configuration Workflow
bullets: FIT: select a case-compatible motherboard form factor.
CONNECT: identify power, expansion, storage, header, and M.2 connections.
COMPATIBILITY: verify CPU socket, chipset/platform, generation, and firmware support.
CONFIGURE: apply the required BIOS/UEFI, security, virtualization, and monitoring settings.
EXPAND: install the card that provides the required function.
COOL: install, power, and verify the correct thermal solution.
sections.callout: FIT → CONNECT → COMPATIBILITY → CONFIGURE → EXPAND → COOL

Multiple processing units in one CPU → multicore
